proved_step: For fixed constants k>0 and alpha>0 with alpha*k<1, suppose a deterministic uniform reduction R maps every length-T input x of L to a SAT instance phi_x of length N(T)=T^{alpha+o(1)}, runs in time o(T/log T), and has decoding and all other simulation overhead o(T/log T). If SAT is decidable in O(N^k), then L is decidable in o(T/log T). Proof: compute R(x), run the SAT algorithm on phi_x, and decode the answer. The total time is o(T/log T)+O((T^{alpha+o(1)})^k)=o(T/log T)+T^{alpha*k+o(1)}. Since alpha*k<1, choose epsilon>0 with alpha*k+epsilon<1; eventually the SAT term is at most T^{alpha*k+epsilon}=o(T/log T), because T^{1-alpha*k-epsilon}/log T tends to infinity. The sum is therefore o(T/log T), contradicting L in DTIME(T)\DTIME(o(T/log T)). At alpha*k=1 this conclusion does not follow: a T^{1+o(1)} upper bound need not be o(T/log T), and even an O(T) SAT-call bound is too large. For a fixed k, a fixed alpha<1/k is admissible only if the corresponding R_alpha is uniformly constructible with all selection, construction, auxiliary-variable, certificate, decoding, and simulation costs covered by the assumed reduction/overhead bounds. Merely having a family indexed by alpha does not handle a nonuniform or unknown choice of k.
